title: About Electrotonus
content: The electrotonic response of a nerve to a subthreshold current pulse has been described as a passive electrical spread in the axolemma since the mid-nineteenth century, and the mathematical formalism of the linear cable equation has been treated as its mechanism ever since Kelvin (1855) and Rall (1957 onwards). We revisit the demonstration that William Rutherford gave to his students at Edinburgh in 1876, restate what he could see and what he could not, and perform three modern in silico experiments in the same demonstrative spirit. The three experiments compare, on the same measured trace, a strict Hodgkin--Huxley formulation, a formulation with independent stimulus and action-potential sources, and a Hodgkin--Huxley formulation augmented ad hoc with variable capacitance and ion-dependent resistance. Only the independent-sources formulation reproduces three routine facts of electrophysiology (all-or-none amplitude, waveform invariance, and coherence of algorithmic artefact subtraction) without a single fitted parameter. We conclude that the electrotonic response is not a passive electrical spread in the axolemma but the vertical projection of a horizontal ionic movement in the periaxonal polyelectrolyte gel adjacent to the axolemma, and that the classical cable equation preserves its descriptive validity as the shadow of that movement while losing its ontological reading as the mechanism.
